lead: A fuel injection system sends the right amount of fuel into each cylinder at the right moment, in a spray fine enough to mix with air. It exists because a carburettor cannot hold a steady air-fuel ratio for every cylinder and load, and because diesel fuel must be injected at high pressure after the air is compressed. It is used on diesel engines of trucks, tractors and generators, and on modern petrol cars with electronic injection. The system must meter, pressurise, time, atomise and distribute the fuel.
prereq: You need chapter 2.1 for the SI mixture requirement, and Unit 1 for the four-stroke cycle.

blocks.text: A fuel injection system has five jobs: meter, atomise, distribute, time and pressurise the fuel. Metering sets the mass of fuel per cycle to match load and speed. Too little fuel gives a lean mixture, misfire and low power. Too much fuel gives black smoke, high fuel consumption and diluted lubricating oil.
Atomisation breaks the fuel into fine droplets. Small droplets expose more surface area to air, so evaporation and mixing are fast. A solid jet burns slowly and deposits carbon.

Distribution gives every cylinder the same fuel quantity and a spray aimed at the right place. Timing starts delivery at the correct crank angle: in a diesel engine near top dead centre (TDC) at the end of compression; in a petrol engine the start depends on port or direct injection. Pressure must push fuel into the cylinder against the compressed air. Diesel injection pressures are high because cylinder pressure at injection is high.

items: Accurate metering: correct mass per cycle and equal between cylinders.
Fine atomisation: small droplets for fast mixing.
Even distribution: same quantity and pattern to each cylinder.
Correct timing: start of delivery at the right crank angle.
Sufficient pressure: fuel enters the cylinder against compressed air.

sections.h3: Types: air, solid, direct and control

blocks.text: Air injection used a blast of compressed air to carry fuel into the cylinder. Early diesel engines used it; the compressor was large and the system slow, and it is obsolete. Solid injection, which some syllabi call airless injection, pressurises the fuel with a pump and forces it through a nozzle. Almost every modern engine uses it.

For diesels, direct injection (DI) sprays fuel straight into a bowl in the piston crown: common rail, unit injector, in-line pump and many distributor-pump engines. Indirect injection (IDI) sprays into a separate prechamber or swirl chamber in the head, joined to the cylinder by a throat; distributor and in-line pumps both feed IDI engines too. For petrol engines the usual words are port (manifold) injection, where fuel meets the air before the inlet valve, and direct injection into the cylinder; some books group port and throttle-body injection under indirect.

By control, a system is mechanical (cam, plunger and spring meter and time the fuel) or electronic (sensors, an electronic control unit, ECU, and solenoid or piezo injectors). By delivery, continuous injection sprays all the time, as in the old mechanical petrol system whose flow was set by an air-flow plate; intermittent injection sprays in timed pulses, as every diesel pump and every modern electronic injector does. The pumps are in Jerk pump, distributor pump and unit injector and the rail in Common rail direct injection.

Injection timing is the crank angle at which the pump starts to deliver fuel. Some texts define it at the nozzle opening. The start of delivery is earlier than the start of spray because of injection lag.

Injection lag is the delay from the start of pump delivery to the nozzle opening. Fuel is slightly compressible, the pressure wave travels along the pipe at about the speed of sound in diesel (near 1400 m/s), and the pressure must build to the nozzle opening pressure. Lag is a time, but the engine turns during it, so it appears as a crank-angle delay of θ = 6 N t degrees, with N in rpm and t in seconds.

Injection duration is the crank angle from nozzle opening to nozzle closing. It grows with fuel quantity. A diesel engine needs injection advance as speed rises so that combustion still starts near TDC. Late injection raises exhaust temperature and smoke; too early injection raises peak pressure and diesel knock. The combustion side is in the topic of CI engine combustion and the delay period.

examples.question: A four-cylinder, four-stroke diesel engine uses 6 kg/h of fuel at 1800 rpm. Find the fuel delivered per injection per cylinder in kg and mg.
steps: A four-stroke cylinder injects once every two revolutions: 1800 ÷ 2 = 900 injections per cylinder per minute; for 4 cylinders, 3600 per minute.
examples.answer: The fuel delivered per injection per cylinder is 2.78×10⁻⁵ kg, or 27.8 mg.
examples.check:
fuel_rate_kg_per_h = 6
rpm = 1800
cylinders = 4
fuel_per_min = fuel_rate_kg_per_h / 60
inj_per_cyl_min = rpm / 2
total_inj_min = cylinders * inj_per_cyl_min
fuel_per_inj_kg = fuel_per_min / total_inj_min
fuel_per_inj_mg = fuel_per_inj_kg * 1e6
print(fuel_per_min)
print(inj_per_cyl_min)
print(total_inj_min)
print(fuel_per_inj_kg)
print(fuel_per_inj_mg)

examples.question: A pump starts delivery at 20° before TDC. The high-pressure pipe is 0.7 m long and the pressure wave travels at 1400 m/s; neglect the time to lift the needle. The nozzle then stays open for 1.5 ms. Find the lag in crank degrees, the nozzle opening and closing angles at 2000 rpm, and the lag at 3000 rpm.
steps: Duration = 12 000 × 0.0015 = 18°, so the nozzle closes at 14° − 18° = −4°, that is 4° after TDC.
At 3000 rpm: lag = 6 × 3000 × 0.0005 = 9.0°, so the nozzle opens at 11° before TDC unless the pump timing is advanced.
examples.answer: Lag 6° at 2000 rpm; the nozzle opens 14° before TDC and closes 4° after TDC. At 3000 rpm the same 0.5 ms costs 9°, which is why injection is advanced with speed.

traps: Direct injection is not the same as direct control. Direct means the injector sprays into the cylinder; it does not mean a lever or human directly controls the fuel.
For a four-stroke engine, each cylinder injects once every two revolutions. Injections per cylinder per minute are rpm ÷ 2, not rpm.
Injection timing is the start of fuel delivery, not the spark timing; spark timing belongs to the ignition system (see Ignition timing and spark advance).
Solid injection and airless injection are the same thing. Air injection is the obsolete air-blast method, not a modern air-assisted petrol injector.
Injection lag is the delay before the nozzle opens; injection duration is the crank angle from opening to closing. Convert either with θ = 6Nt, not 360Nt.

quiz.q: List the five requirements of a fuel injection system.
quiz.a: Accurate metering, fine atomisation, even distribution, correct timing and sufficient pressure.

quiz.q: Why does a solid injection system not need a compressed-air blast?
quiz.a: A pump raises the fuel to high pressure. The pressure energy forces the fuel through small nozzle holes and breaks it into droplets. No separate compressed air is needed.

quiz.q: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine runs at 2400 rpm and uses 9.6 kg/h of fuel. Find the fuel per injection per cylinder in mg.
quiz.a: Fuel rate = 9.6 ÷ 60 = 0.16 kg/min. Injections per cylinder per minute = 2400 ÷ 2 = 1200. Total injections per minute = 4 × 1200 = 4800. Fuel per injection = 0.16 ÷ 4800 = 3.333×10⁻⁵ kg = 33.33 mg.

quiz.q: A pump-line-nozzle diesel has a 0.4 ms injection lag. Why does an engine that starts delivery at a fixed crank angle inject later and later as speed rises?
quiz.a: The lag is a fixed time, so its crank angle 6Nt grows with speed: 4.8° at 2000 rpm and 9.6° at 4000 rpm. Fixed delivery timing therefore starts the spray later at speed, and combustion moves past TDC; an automatic timing advance or an electronic system corrects it.

quiz.q: Define injection timing and injection lag.
quiz.a: Injection timing is the crank angle at which the pump starts to deliver fuel. Injection lag is the delay from pump delivery to nozzle opening.

quiz.q: Why is injection lag not equal to injection duration?
quiz.a: Lag is the delay before the nozzle opens. Duration is the time the nozzle stays open. Lag depends on pressure wave speed, fuel compressibility and spring load; duration depends mainly on fuel quantity and pump delivery rate.

quiz.q: Classify common rail, unit injector, a prechamber diesel and petrol port injection as direct or indirect.
quiz.a: Common rail: direct. Unit injector: direct. Prechamber diesel: indirect. Petrol port injection: port (manifold) injection, grouped as indirect in some books.

beyond: Not for the exam. Common-rail diesels use pilot and post injections to cut noise and NOx, and piezo injectors open faster than solenoid ones. Search terms: injection rate shaping, needle lift sensor, pressure wave in injection lines.
